Passengers walk past firefighters at a Green Line station in Boston after the trolley collision Friday evening. The trolley driver has told investigators he was text messaging during Friday night's collision, which injured 20 people. The Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority, which previously had banned operators from using cell phones and other portable devices, now has told employees to leave the devices at home while on duty, National Transportation Safety Board member Debbie Hersman said Monday. Hersman also noted investigators have determined that the operator may have missed some crucial indications of a stopped trolley ahead on the tracks.  Watch new transit rule on cell phones » . "The operator of the striking train was interviewed at the hospital by two detectives," said MBTA general manager Daniel Grabauskas. "He admitted that he was texting at the time of the accident." The operator told detectives that, when he looked up, "it was too late as he applied the brake and the train struck the other trolley," Grabauskas said. He described himself as "outraged." # MBTA Trolley Operator Was Texting Before Boston Crash That Injured Dozens, NTSB Finds

**BOSTON (CNN)** — A Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority trolley operator was actively texting on a personal cell phone in the moments before a Green Line trolley collided with another train during evening rush hour, according to a preliminary report released Thursday by the National Transportation Safety Board.

The crash, which occurred last month near the Kenmore Square station, sent 27 passengers to area hospitals with injuries ranging from minor cuts and bruises to broken bones. Two passengers remain hospitalized in stable condition, MBTA officials said.

According to the NTSB report, data pulled from the trolley's onboard event recorder showed the operator, whose name has not been released, sent and received several text messages in the two minutes leading up to the collision. Cell phone records corroborate that a personal device was in use at the time of impact.

"Our preliminary findings indicate the operator was not maintaining the required visual attention to the track ahead," said NTSB investigator Sarah Chen at a press briefing Thursday. "Phone records show message activity within seconds of the collision. This is consistent with what we call inattentional blindness — the operator's eyes may have been open, but their attention was diverted from the operating environment."

Chen emphasized that the investigation is ongoing and a final determination of probable cause could take up to a year, but she noted the findings so far point clearly toward human error rather than mechanical failure.

"At this stage, we have found no evidence of brake malfunction, signal failure, or track defect," Chen said. "The safety systems performed as designed. What we are looking closely at is the human factor."

The trolley involved was traveling inbound when it struck the rear of a stopped train ahead of it. Witnesses described a loud impact and passengers being thrown from their seats.

"I heard screeching, and then everyone just went flying," said passenger Maria Delgado, who was riding home from work. "It happened so fast. People were screaming, and there was glass everywhere near the front."

MBTA General Manager Phillip Eng addressed reporters outside the agency's headquarters, calling the findings "deeply troubling" and pledging full cooperation with federal investigators.

"Safety is our top priority, and any violation of our strict no-phone policy for operators is unacceptable," Eng said. "The operator involved has been placed on administrative leave pending the outcome of this investigation. We are also conducting an immediate, system-wide review of our policies and enforcement mechanisms around personal device use."

Eng said the MBTA maintains a zero-tolerance policy prohibiting operators from using personal electronic devices while a vehicle is in motion, a rule reinforced through regular training. He acknowledged, however, that the incident has raised questions about how consistently that policy is monitored and enforced.

"We owe it to our riders to be transparent about what happened here," Eng said. "This should not have occurred, and we are taking a hard look at what additional safeguards — whether technological or procedural — can help ensure it never happens again."

The NTSB said it is also examining whether the MBTA's existing distraction-prevention measures, including any device-detection technology on trains, were adequate or in use at the time of the crash.

Advocacy groups have renewed calls for stricter federal regulations on distracted operation across all forms of public transit, not just roadways.

"We've made real progress on distracted driving laws for cars and trucks," said Jonathan Reyes, a transit safety advocate with the group Riders First. "But when it comes to buses, trolleys and trains carrying dozens or hundreds of people at a time, the stakes are even higher. This crash is a wake-up call."

The MBTA said it is offering counseling resources to affected passengers and reviewing surveillance and operator conduct footage from other lines as part of an internal audit.

The NTSB's full investigation, including its final report and safety recommendations, is expected to be completed within the next several months. In the meantime, officials urged patience from the public as both agencies work to determine what changes might prevent similar incidents in the future.

"Every one of these investigations is about more than just this one crash," Chen said. "It's about the thousands of people who ride transit every single day and trust that the person at the controls is fully focused on getting them home safely."

**BOSTON** — A Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) trolley operator has admitted to texting on a personal cell phone moments before a collision that injured dozens of passengers, transit officials confirmed this week.

The accident occurred when the Green Line trolley rear-ended another train that had stopped ahead of it. Emergency responders treated approximately 46 people for injuries, though none were reported life-threatening. Passengers described a sudden jolt and the sound of screeching brakes moments before impact.

## Driver's Admission

The operator, whose identity has not been publicly released pending investigation, told MBTA officials and National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigators that he had been sending a text message in the moments leading up to the crash. He has reportedly been suspended without pay pending further review and potential disciplinary action, including possible termination.

MBTA General Manager officials expressed alarm at the admission, noting that transit operators are strictly prohibited from using personal electronic devices while trains are in motion.

## Echoes of Past Tragedies

This incident bears troubling similarities to a 2008 Chatsworth, California commuter train crash, in which a Metrolink engineer was found to have been texting immediately before his train collided head-on with a freight train, killing 25 people and injuring more than 130 others. Investigators later discovered the engineer had a pattern of texting while operating trains, and the tragedy prompted sweeping changes in rail safety regulations, including the mandated installation of positive train control (PTC) systems nationwide.

The Chatsworth disaster became a landmark case in transportation safety, spurring the federal Rail Safety Improvement Act of 2008, which set deadlines for implementing anti-collision technology across the U.S. rail system.

Transit safety advocates say the Boston incident raises fresh questions about whether enough has been done in the years since to curb distracted operation among transit employees, despite stricter policies and increased training.

## Renewed Calls for Accountability

"This is exactly the kind of preventable tragedy we thought we'd addressed after Chatsworth," said one transportation safety analyst. "Policies exist on paper, but enforcement and a culture of accountability are what actually save lives."

The MBTA said it will review its cell phone policy enforcement mechanisms, including potential use of cab-facing cameras and stricter monitoring systems already implemented by some transit agencies nationwide.

The NTSB investigation is ongoing, and further details about additional safety failures, if any, are expected in a preliminary report within the coming weeks.

# Trolley Crash on MBTA Green Line Prompts Signal System Overhaul, Operator Review

**BOSTON (CNN)** — The Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority is implementing sweeping safety changes following a trolley collision on the Green Line that injured several passengers and renewed scrutiny of the transit system's aging infrastructure and safety protocols.

The crash occurred during evening rush hour when a Green Line trolley struck the rear of another train that had stopped ahead of it near a station platform. Preliminary findings from the MBTA and the National Transportation Safety Board point to a combination of factors: a malfunctioning signal system that failed to alert the trailing operator to slow down, combined with what investigators describe as a delayed response from that operator.

## Signal Failure Under Scrutiny

According to internal MBTA reports, the automatic block signal system in the affected section of track had a documented history of intermittent failures dating back several months. Maintenance logs reviewed by investigators show at least three prior incidents in which the same signal segment reported inaccurate readings, though repairs were characterized as temporary fixes rather than full system replacements.

"This is not simply a case of one signal malfunctioning on one day," said a transit safety analyst briefed on the investigation. "There's a pattern here of deferred maintenance on a signal system that is decades old in parts of the network."

The MBTA's Green Line, one of the oldest light rail systems in the country, has faced longstanding criticism over infrastructure investment, with portions of its signal equipment reportedly dating back to the 1980s and earlier.

## Operator Response Questioned

Beyond the mechanical failure, investigators say data from the trolley's event recorder indicates the operator did not begin braking until several seconds after the preceding train came into view — a delay that safety officials say exceeded standard reaction protocols even accounting for the signal malfunction.

The operator has been placed on administrative leave pending the outcome of the investigation. The MBTA has not released the employee's name, and their union representative has said the operator was "following training as understood at the time" and that systemic signal issues bear primary responsibility.

## Passenger Accounts

Passengers aboard the trolley described a sudden, forceful impact with little warning.

"There was no announcement, no slowdown that I noticed — then suddenly we were thrown forward," said one rider treated at the scene for minor injuries. Emergency responders transported several passengers to area hospitals; MBTA officials said none of the injuries were considered life-threatening.

## Policy Changes Announced

In response, MBTA General Manager's office announced a series of immediate and longer-term measures:

- **Accelerated signal replacement**: Funding has been redirected to expedite replacement of aging block signal components along the Green Line, with a completion target of within two years rather than the previously scheduled five.
- **Mandatory retraining**: All light rail operators will undergo refresher training on manual braking protocols and emergency response procedures within the signal system.
- **Independent safety audit**: The MBTA has commissioned a third-party review of its entire signal maintenance history, to be completed within 90 days.
- **Real-time monitoring system**: New sensors are being installed to provide dispatchers with live alerts when block signals report anomalies, rather than relying solely on scheduled inspections.

## Broader Context

The incident adds to a string of safety concerns that have dogged the MBTA in recent years, including federal oversight actions and prior NTSB findings citing inadequate safety culture within the agency. The Federal Transit Administration had previously issued directives requiring the MBTA to address deferred maintenance backlogs system-wide.

Massachusetts Governor's office issued a statement saying the administration is "committed to ensuring the T has the resources and oversight needed to guarantee rider safety," while transit advocates called for more transparency around maintenance records going forward.

The NTSB's full investigation is expected to take several months, with a preliminary report anticipated within 30 days.
